message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Symbol** | H |
| **Common isotopes** | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %) – stable; H‑3 (tritium) – radioactive (half‑life ≈12.3 y) |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average weighted by natural abundance) |
| **Molecular formula** | H₂ (diatomic gas under normal conditions) |
| **Molar mass** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ (for H₂) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 g cm⁻³) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14 K) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Standard enthalpy of formation** | ΔH°f = 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition for elemental H₂) |
| **Standard entropy** | S°(298 K) = 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (for H₂) |
| **Standard molar volume** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Second ionization energy** | 24.587 eV (2375 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | 72.80 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative value indicates energy release when gaining an electron) |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ (≈4.52 eV per bond) |
| **Heat capacity (Cp, 298 K)** | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (for H₂) |
| **Thermal conductivity (300 K)** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (for H₂) |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals (e.g., NaH, CaH₂), reacts with halogens (forming HX), oxidizes to water (combustion: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O). |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; explosive limits in air: 4 %–75 % (volume) |
| **Solubility in water** | 1.6 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0016 mol L⁻¹) – very low |
| **Spectral lines** | Strong Balmer series visible (e.g., Hα at 656.3 nm) – basis for astronomical detection |
| **Uses** | Fuel cell reactant, rocket propellant (liquid H₂ + liquid O₂), ammonia synthesis (Haber process), hydrogenation reactions, metal hydride storage, laboratory standard gas. |

**General Notes**

- Hydrogen is the *lightest* element (atomic mass ≈1 u) and the most abundant in the universe (≈75 % of all atoms).
- It exists naturally as a diatomic molecule (H₂) under ambient conditions; it can also exist as atomic hydrogen (H•) in plasma or high‑temperature environments.
- Its small size and high ionization energy make it a good reducing agent in many industrial processes.
- Isotopic substitution (D₂, T₂) alters kinetic isotope effects, useful in mechanistic studies and in nuclear fusion research (T + D → He + n).

These values are taken from standard thermodynamic tables (e.g., NIST-JANAF, CRC Handbook) and represent typical reference data for pure hydrogen gas at 298 K and 1 atm.
